      <title>Chelsea are the Premier League’s most fun team but is it sustainable?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/who-scored-blog/2026/oct/15/chelsea-premier-league-fun-team-sustainable-xabi-alonso-europe</link>
      <description><p>Xabi Alonso’s side are scoring and conceding at a remarkable rate. It’s great for neutrals but not necessarily the best way to qualify for Europe</p><p>By <a href="https://www.whoscored.com/">WhoScored</a></p><p>Watching Chelsea this season ought to come with a health warning. Goals arrive in abundance, leads are established before spectators have settled into their seats and clean sheets have become an alien concept. Xabi Alonso has transformed Chelsea into one of the Premier League’s most thrilling spectacles. They have scored 15 goals and conceded 13. That’s 4.7 goals per game in six matches. Chelsea are a neutral’s dream, but is it sustainable?</p><p>They have scored 15 goals from an expected goals total of just 8.4, an over-performance of 6.6. An 18.3% conversion rate is second only to Manchester City’s 19.1%, while eight of their 15 goals have come from shots with xG below 0.13. The five goals against Bournemouth last weekend came from an xG of just 0.75.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/who-scored-blog/2026/oct/15/chelsea-premier-league-fun-team-sustainable-xabi-alonso-europe">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Why most Manchester City fans stand by their club | Letters</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/13/why-most-manchester-city-fans-stand-by-their-club</link>
      <description><p><strong>Andrew Burton </strong>suspects that had other teams delivered similar success, fans would have been just as forgiving of their owners</p><p>Re Sean Ingle’s article (<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/05/how-do-sports-fans-end-up-as-aggressive-defenders-of-a-nation-states-regime">How did some City fans become aggressive defenders of a nation state’s regime?, 5 October</a>), I suspect that most City fans are no more supportive of the United Arab Emirates regime than those of Arsenal were of the Rwandan government during its sponsorship deal, or Newcastle’s of Saudi Arabia, or those of the <a href="https://www.bigissue.com/news/social-justice/premier-league-clubs-shirt-sponsors-gambling-companies/">11 clubs</a> whose shirt sponsors were gambling companies in 2025-26. Fans are simply concerned with how their club is managed and success on the pitch.</p><p>At City, UAE ownership brought unprecedented success to a historic club. The new regime delivered the most feted coach of our time, who revolutionised how the game in England was played. Highly successful City youth teams nurtured young talent that has gone on to grace numerous other squads in the Premier League and beyond, including England players.&nbsp;City Women, reigning double winners, are the current force in English women’s football.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/13/why-most-manchester-city-fans-stand-by-their-club">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Coventry City 4-1 Newcastle United: Premier League – as it happened</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/live/2026/oct/12/coventry-city-newcastle-united-premier-league-live-score-updates</link>
      <description><p>Goals from Jack Rudoni, Sidiki Cherif, Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni – Cherif’s and Mfuni’s blinders – gave Coventry their first Premier League home win in 25 years</p><p><strong>So where is our game? </strong>Coventry will want to use their wide attackers to get them up the pitch. Down their left in particular, I’d expect to see Dasilva and Mason-Clark ganging up on Miley, who isn’t a full-back, with Rudoni and Yirkenkyi making late runs to give them presence in the box. I also wonder if Cherif will look to run off Botman, who isn’t the quickest, with Thomas-Asante and Van Ewijk looking to supply him with crosses.</p><p><strong>Email! </strong>“I say this is a perfect fixture,” writes Mary Waltz. “To get back to semi normal football. We have had a week to focus on the City problem but let’s get real. Whatever happens to them it will probably months before the lawyers get all their billable hours in and we don’t know what the final outcome will be. I for one am tired of speculating when it is pointless until<em> </em>the powers that be make up their minds.<em> Let’s play ball.</em>”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/live/2026/oct/12/coventry-city-newcastle-united-premier-league-live-score-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Manchester City unrepentant in victory, Spurs make progress of a sort and Noni Madueke meets the moment</p><p>The manner of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/11/liverpool-manchester-city-premier-league-match-report">Manchester City’s victory at Liverpool</a> was an article of both vindication and vilification.       <description><p>There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms</p><p>Football, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863.
